The old abandoned house at the end of the street held a secret that no one had ever discovered. I know, because I spent thirty years walking past it twice a day and never once looked at it properly, and that is how secrets survive.

It was number 14, the last house before the road gave up and became field. Slate roof going green. A porch with a swing that had rotted to a slant, though the boards beneath it were sound—that was the thing about 14 Rosewood. Nothing about it was quite as broken as it looked. The roses along the fence bloomed every June without a soul to prune them. The gutters never sagged. And the porch light came on at dusk.

That was the part people argued about. It came on at dusk, every evening, a small yellow stubbornness in a house the county had listed as vacant since 1961. My father said it was the wind on a loose wire. My mother said it was a reflection off the water tower. Our neighbor Mrs. Pruitt said it was Mr. Wexler, who had buried something in the cellar and never left, and then she laughed in a way that meant she believed it.

When I was nine, Kevin Marsh bet me a dollar I couldn't touch the front door.

I made it to the porch. That was all. I stood on the top step with my fist raised and the smell came out through the mail slot at me—cold dust and lemon peel, and underneath it something warm, like a kettle that had only just stopped. The hair went up on my arms. I ran. Kevin kept his dollar and I kept the smell, and for years afterward I could summon it exactly, the way you can summon a face.

Then my father got sick, and I came home, and for a while that was the whole of my life: the gray front room, the pills sorted into a plastic box, the slow arithmetic of a man going out like a lamp.

One evening I stood on my own porch with a cup of tea and watched the light come on down the street. Then I walked to it.

The door wasn't locked. That was the first impossibility; the second was the smell, exactly as I remembered it, and no dust at all. Cold and lemon and warmth. A bowl of keys sat on the hall table like someone had just come in. The wallpaper was small blue flowers. In the parlor a clock had stopped at seven past four, and beside it a newspaper lay folded to the twelfth of August, 1961, and beside that a cake on a plate with a knife laid across it, uncut, the icing gone the color of old ivory.

I should have been frightened. Instead I felt the particular shame of a person who has walked past a thing for thirty years and called it empty.

The hallway had five doors. Four gave onto rooms that were ordinary and clean and waiting—bed made, window open, a child's shoe beneath a chair. The fifth was narrow and closed, and set into it at knee height was a mail slot, brass, worn to a shine on the inside.

The room behind it had shelves, and the shelves had letters.

Hundreds of them. Thousands, maybe, in bundles tied with string that had gone slack. All of them addressed the same way, in pencil and fountain pen and one in crayon: *14 Rosewood Lane.* None of them opened. Every flap still sealed.

On the desk lay a ledger, unlined, hand-ruled. Names and dates down the left, and a few words down the right.

*Mrs. Calder, 1962 — the rent.*
*T. Okafor, 1978 — a place to sleep that winter.*
*The Ellis girl, 1989 — the dog, found.*

And then, halfway down a page in my own nine-year-old handwriting:

*Rowan Teale, 9 May 1993 — that my mother stays.*

I had to sit down on the floor. I had written that. I remembered the pencil, the torn page from my spelling book, the walk in the dark with my heart going like a bird in a jar, and the slot swallowing it, and running home, and never telling anyone, not once.

My mother left in the September of that year.

She stayed until I was twelve.

"I never read them."

She was in the doorway. An old woman in slippers, hair pinned up, holding a cup of tea that steamed.

"People write down what they can't say out loud," she said, "and they push it through, and they walk away lighter. They think the house does the rest. Mostly the house is just a place to put a thing." She nodded at the ledger. "But sometimes a body can act on it. Somebody has to be here to hear the slot. That's all it's ever been. One person, listening."

"Who are you?"

"Ada. My father kept it before me, from '61. His sister kept it before him." She set the tea down beside the cake and did not cut it. "There's always one. The house is particular. It picks someone who left a letter and never came back to ask what happened."

I looked at the shelves. At all of those unopened lives. "And my mother?"

"Your mother got three years she hadn't planned on." Ada's voice was not unkind. "A house can't hold a person. It can only hold a door open a while longer. It's not much. It's what there is."

I asked her how long she'd been alone in it. She said, "Long enough to forget I was," and laughed, and it was the same laugh as Mrs. Pruitt's, and I understood it at last.

She gave me the key anyway, when I left. Pressed it into my palm whether I wanted it or not.

"You don't have to decide tonight," she said. "Only don't let the light go out."

I walked home under the lime trees. My father's window was lit, and behind me the porch light at 14 Rosewood was lit, and the street lay quiet in the way a street lies quiet when it is holding its breath.

It's on now. That's all I'll say about that.

But if you're ever walking past at dusk, and there's something in you that you can't say to a living soul—the door at the end of the street has a slot, and the hinges are oiled, and no one will ever ask your name."}
